analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale, manufacture, and possession of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Rep. David Cicilline with 194 cosponsors—all Democrats—was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a vote or a hearing before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and magazines holding more than 15 rounds. People who already owned such weapons could keep them, and hundreds of hunting and sporting guns were explicitly exempted by name. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The bill's benefits would have gone to the general public, and especially to people in schools, workplaces, stores, and public gatherings where mass shootings with these weapons occur, through a reduced supply of new semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines. Existing owners were protected: anyone who lawfully possessed a covered weapon before enactment could keep it, and hunters and sport shooters were shielded by a long list of exempted models.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary people exposed to mass shootings

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines, the firearms most often used in high-fatality mass shootings.
Grandfathers existing owners: people who lawfully own covered weapons can keep them, and can still sell or transfer them through a licensed dealer with a background check.
Exempts hundreds of hunting and sporting firearms by name, plus manually operated, antique, rimfire, and permanently inoperable firearms.
Requires secure storage of grandfathered weapons, serial numbers and manufacture dates on new weapons and magazines, and lets states use federal justice grants to fund buy-backs.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would have fallen on firearms manufacturers and dealers, who would lose the legal market for a wide range of popular semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns, and on gun owners who could no longer sell or transfer covered weapons except through a licensed dealer with a background check.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers an enormous range of common semiautomatic firearms: any semiautomatic rifle with a detachable magazine plus one feature such as a pistol grip, threaded barrel, or barrel shroud, plus hundreds of specifically named models, including many pistols and shotguns.

Grandfathered weapons could still be owned but future sales and transfers between private parties would have required a licensed dealer and a background check, and owners would have faced secure-storage requirements—costs and legal exposure falling on lawful owners.

Opponents' core objection is that the bill defines banned weapons by features and model names rather than function, sweeping in firearms used widely for target shooting, home defense, and hunting, and criminalizing ordinary commerce in them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—fewer or less deadly mass shootings and a nationwide sales ban on the weapons that recur in them—came at real costs opponents would flag honestly: it criminalized the sale of very popular rifles that millions of Americans own and use legally, and critics argued the feature-based definition covered guns by cosmetics rather than function. Gun owners who already had such weapons could keep them, but could only sell them through licensed dealers with background checks, adding friction and cost. The deeper cost in this case was the bill's fate: it was never even debated, so no compromise was forged and the policy question was left unanswered.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The Assault Weapons Ban of 2023 was introduced in the House on February 1, 2023 and referred to the Judiciary Committee.
The complete action history shows only the introduction, the referral to Judiciary, and a June 2023 change of first sponsor from Rep. Cicilline to Rep. McBath—no hearings, no markup, no floor vote.
The bill had 194 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no Republican support.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and dealers kept the assault-weapon market open, and current owners face no new restrictions; no one secured the ban's proposed safety benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers, dealers, and current owners

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors—every one of them a Democrat.

against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred on February 1, 2023.

against.name: House Republicans (majority)
against.what_they_did: Held majority control of the House and its committees after January 2023; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and the majority's committees declined to act on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 194 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans supported the bill, and the Republican-controlled House never advanced it.

industries.note: The bill bans future manufacture and sale of a large share of the semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns that are the industry's best-selling products, including the AR-15 and AK-style platforms. Retailers would lose a major product line; only existing inventory could be transferred with background checks.
New sales of covered weapons end, but the bill makes licensed dealers the required channel for all future transfers of grandfathered weapons, giving them a regulated role in the secondary market.
